prompt: In moto, a user with no permissions at all deletes a bucket, and the call succeeds. What does that prove about AWS?
hint: Think about what moto checks before you turn its checking on.

choices.text: That AWS would allow it too, since moto answers in AWS's own format
choices.why: The format of an answer says nothing about the decision behind it. moto imitates the shape and, out of the box, skips the judgement.

choices.text: Nothing: moto allows every call until its own checking is turned on
choices.why: Right. Lesson 7 turns the checking on. Before that, a success in moto is not evidence that a policy would allow the action.

choices.text: That the bucket had no policy of its own
choices.why: Even with a bucket policy, moto does not judge it. The success comes from moto checking nothing, not from what the bucket carried.

choices.text: That deleting a bucket needs no permission in AWS
choices.why: Every action in AWS needs a permission, and deleting a bucket is one of the most guarded. moto simply did not ask.

prompt: Where does every price quoted in this course come from?
hint: moto is not a shop.

choices.text: From what moto reports after each command it answers in the lab
choices.why: moto sends no bill and knows no price. Whatever it says about cost is not AWS's.

choices.text: From a real account's bill
choices.why: There is no real account behind the course, so there is no bill to read.

choices.text: From AWS's public price list, a set of JSON files
choices.why: Right. The list is a set of JSON files anyone may download, and each version is kept, so a price can be pinned.

prompt: Which of these does moto 5.2.3 NOT enforce, even with its permission checking turned on? Choose all that apply.
hint: Four lines of the section's list, and one of them is enforced.

choices.text: A permission boundary on a user
choices.why: Right. moto stores the boundary and ignores it; lesson 8 teaches it from AWS's documentation.

choices.text: A service control policy attached to an account
choices.why: Right. moto records the policy in the organisation and lets the call through anyway.

choices.text: An explicit deny in the user's own policy
choices.why: This one moto does enforce: an explicit deny in an identity policy refuses the call.

choices.text: A bucket's own policy denying a deletion
choices.why: Right. A resource-based policy is not judged by moto, so the bucket is deleted.

prompt: moto is stopped with Ctrl+C at the end of a session and started again the next day. What does it hold?
hint: Where does moto keep what it is told?

choices.text: Nothing; it starts empty
choices.why: Right. moto keeps its state in memory and forgets it when it stops, which is why each lesson starts clean.

choices.text: Everything created the day before, read back from `~/aws`
choices.why: Nothing is written to `~/aws` by moto. The directory holds the tools and `env.sh`, not moto's state.

choices.text: Only the IAM users, which are kept apart from the other services
choices.why: IAM is in memory like every other service in moto, and goes with the rest.

choices.text: The default VPC and nothing else
choices.why: moto does make a default VPC again, but on demand, the way AWS has one in every region. It is not a survivor of the day before.

prompt: A student on a Mac with Apple silicon wants the transcripts to match. Which path does the section recommend?
hint: The tools run on macOS; the messages are another matter.

choices.text: Install the tools directly on macOS, where both of them also run
choices.why: They would run, but the system's own messages would not match transcripts recorded on Ubuntu.

choices.text: Ubuntu in a virtual machine
choices.why: Right. A virtual machine gives the same system the lessons were recorded on, and the Arm processor needs the Arm file.

choices.text: AWS CloudShell in the browser
choices.why: CloudShell needs an AWS account, and the course is built to need none.

choices.text: WSL, the same as on Windows
choices.why: WSL is a Windows feature. A Mac has no WSL.

prompt: `env.sh` sets `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=test` and `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=test`. Why those values rather than none?
hint: What happens to a request that reaches AWS by mistake?

choices.text: moto refuses requests that carry no credentials, and AWS would accept these
choices.why: It is the other way round for AWS: it refused these exact values in the section on failures.

choices.text: They are moto's administrator key, which unlocks every service
choices.why: moto has no administrator key. Until its checking is on it accepts any credentials at all.

choices.text: Requests get signed, and AWS refuses these
choices.why: Right. Without credentials the command line refuses to send anything; with placeholders, a request that escapes to AWS is refused there.

prompt: `env.sh` sends every request of the AWS command line to moto by setting `AWS_ENDPOINT_URL` to `http://localhost:___`.
hint: The port moto listens on.

prompt: Put the steps of a working session in order, starting from a computer where the lab is installed.
hint: The server has to be up before the client can ask it anything.
trap: Starting moto before reading `env.sh` is the usual slip: `moto_server` is in the virtual environment, which `env.sh` switches on.

prompt: A colleague adds a real access key to `env.sh` 'to save time later'. Which risk does the section name?
hint: The file is read into every terminal of the course, and lives in a home directory.

choices.text: A file in a home directory reaches backups, shared folders and screenshots
choices.why: Right. A secret in a file is copied wherever the file goes, without anybody deciding it should be.

choices.text: moto would reject the key and stop answering
choices.why: Until its checking is on, moto accepts any key. The danger is not moto's.

choices.text: The real key would be sent to moto, which publishes what it receives
choices.why: A request signed with a key does not carry the secret half of it, and moto publishes nothing.

choices.text: The AWS command line refuses to read a key from an environment variable
choices.why: It reads keys from the environment every day; that is exactly how the `test` values reach it.

prompt: Match each line of `env.sh` to what it does.
hint: One job each.

pairs.right: names São Paulo as the region

prompt: `aws sts get-caller-identity` answers `Could not connect to the endpoint URL: "http://localhost:4567/"`. What is the first thing to look at?
hint: The address in the message is the right one.

choices.text: Whether `env.sh` was read in this terminal
choices.why: It was: the command line used the address `env.sh` sets. Without it, the request would have gone to AWS.

choices.text: The terminal running moto
choices.why: Right. Nothing answered on port 4567, so moto is stopped, or it stopped with an error it printed there.

choices.text: The credentials, which AWS has refused
choices.why: A refusal of credentials is an answer. Here nothing answered at all.

choices.text: The version of the AWS command line
choices.why: Any version would print the same, because the problem is on the other side of the connection.

prompt: After `unset AWS_ENDPOINT_URL`, the same command answers `InvalidClientTokenId`. Who refused the request?
hint: Where does the command line send a request when no endpoint is set?

choices.text: moto, because the placeholder key expired
choices.why: moto never saw it. And `test` does not expire; moto accepts it every time.

choices.text: The command line itself, before sending anything
choices.why: The command line had credentials to sign with, so it sent the request. The error names an operation AWS answered.

choices.text: AWS's own token service in São Paulo
choices.why: Right. With no endpoint the request goes to AWS, which has no key called `test`. Nothing was created or charged.

prompt: `moto_server -p 4567` prints `Address already in use`. What is the likeliest cause?
hint: The message says the port has an owner.

choices.text: A moto started earlier is still running
choices.why: Right. Find its terminal and stop it with Ctrl+C, or close that terminal.

choices.text: The virtual environment was not activated
choices.why: Then `moto_server` would not be found at all. This one ran and found the port taken.

choices.text: Port 4567 is reserved by Ubuntu for AWS
choices.why: Ubuntu reserves nothing for AWS. Something on this computer is listening there.

choices.text: `env.sh` names a different port from the one typed
choices.why: A different port would not stop the server from starting. It would start, and the command line would miss it.

prompt: The AWS installer fails with `Exec format error`. What does `uname -m` help decide?
hint: Two files, two kinds of processor.

choices.text: Whether the virtual environment is active in this terminal
choices.why: `uname -m` knows nothing of Python. It prints the processor's architecture.

choices.text: Which version of Ubuntu is installed
choices.why: That is `lsb_release` or `/etc/os-release`. The zip is the same for every Ubuntu.

choices.text: Which of the two zip files to download
choices.why: Right. The installer is built for one processor, and an Arm machine needs the Arm file.

prompt: Put the first hour of a new AWS account in the order the section gives.
hint: Protect what can lose everything first; spend nothing until you would hear about it.
items: turn on MFA for the root user
decline to create a root access key
create a budget with an alert
make an everyday identity and stop using root
trap: Making the everyday identity before the budget is the usual slip: anything that identity creates can cost money before an alert exists.

prompt: A budget alert fires at 80% of the month's budget. What happens to the resources that are spending?
hint: What is an alert for?

choices.text: AWS stops them until the next month
choices.why: A budget does not stop anything by itself. That is the misunderstanding that lets bills grow.

choices.text: Nothing; somebody is told, and has to act
choices.why: Right. An alert informs. That is why it comes first, while the amount is still small.

choices.text: They move to the free tier
choices.why: Nothing moves to a free tier. The free tier is a set of allowances, not a place resources go.

choices.text: The card is charged in advance for the rest of the month
choices.why: AWS bills what was used, after it was used. An alert changes nothing about the charge.

prompt: Why does the section advise a separate terminal that never reads `env.sh` for a real account?
hint: What would `env.sh` do to a command meant for AWS?

choices.text: Because the real account rejects any terminal that ran moto
choices.why: AWS cannot see which terminal sent a request. It sees the request.

choices.text: So that which AWS a command reaches is decided by the window, not by a variable somebody has to remember
choices.why: Right. In a moto terminal every command goes to moto; in the other, to AWS. Two prompts are harder to confuse than one set of variables.

choices.text: Because `env.sh` deletes credentials it finds in the environment
choices.why: It sets placeholders, which replace whatever was there, but deleting is not its job; the point is the endpoint.

choices.text: Because the AWS command line can only hold one account per computer
choices.why: It holds as many as there are profiles, which lesson 25 shows.

prompt: Which statement about an Availability Zone is right?
hint: It is about failure, not about a building.

choices.text: One datacentre, and a region is that datacentre with its backups
choices.why: This is the common wrong picture. A zone may be several buildings, and a region is several zones.

choices.text: One or more datacentres with their own power and network, isolated from the other zones
choices.why: Right. The separation is the point: one zone can fail while the next keeps running.

choices.text: A city where AWS runs a few of its services and has no region of its own
choices.why: That describes a Local Zone, which extends a region into a city.

prompt: The shop's account puts its database in `sa-east-1a`. The payments account, a different account, wants its client in the same physical zone. What should the two teams agree on?
hint: One of the two names is the same in every account.

choices.text: The zone name, `sa-east-1a`, since both accounts are in the same region
choices.why: A zone name can map to a different physical zone in each account, so both could say `sa-east-1a` and sit in different buildings.

choices.text: The zone id, such as `sae1-az1`
choices.why: Right. The id names the same zone everywhere; `describe-availability-zones` prints the name each account uses for it.

choices.text: Nothing; AWS places related accounts in the same zone
choices.why: AWS knows nothing about which accounts are related unless you tell it, and placement is still per account.

choices.text: The CIDR range of the subnet each of them uses
choices.why: A CIDR range says which addresses, not which zone. Two accounts can use the same range in different zones.

prompt: A zone that extends a region into a city where AWS has no region, such as `us-west-2-lax-1a`, is a ___ Zone.
hint: Its name says how near it is.

prompt: moto answered `describe-availability-zones --all-availability-zones` for `us-west-2` with four ordinary zones. What does that say about AWS?
hint: What does moto carry, and what does it leave out?

choices.text: That `us-west-2` has no Local Zones
choices.why: It has the most of any region. moto simply carries none.

choices.text: That Local Zones need an opt-in before `--all-availability-zones` shows them
choices.why: `--all-availability-zones` lists them opted in or not, with their status. The absence is moto's.

choices.text: Little: moto carries no Local Zones, so the answer is about moto
choices.why: Right. Against AWS the same command adds the Local Zones with `local-zone` as their type; that part was not run here.

prompt: A database sends 500 GB a month to a standby in another zone of `sa-east-1`. At the list's price, how many dollars a month is the transfer, counting both sides?
hint: 0.01 per GB, charged leaving one zone and arriving in the other.

prompt: A nightly copy adds up to 2,048 GB a month sent from `sa-east-1` to `us-east-1`. At 0.138 dollars per GB, what does the month cost?
hint: Gigabytes times the price.

prompt: The backups of a shop in São Paulo must have a copy in another region. Which fact from the price list should shape the design?
hint: Read the two directions of the same crossing.

choices.text: Leaving São Paulo costs 0.138 per GB and leaving Virginia 0.02, so the copy is paid going out
choices.why: Right. The price follows the direction, and the copy is paid on every byte that leaves São Paulo, every day.

choices.text: Transfer between regions is free inside one account
choices.why: The account changes nothing here. The regional lines are charged whoever owns both ends.

choices.text: Data in from the internet is free, so the copy should travel over the internet
choices.why: It would still leave São Paulo to the internet, at 0.15 per GB, which is dearer than the regional line.

choices.text: Between zones costs 0.01, so a second zone is as good as a second region
choices.why: A zone is cheaper and is still inside the region; it does not survive the loss of the region, which is what the copy is for.

prompt: Match each crossing from `sa-east-1` to its price per GB in the list of 16 September 2026.
hint: Four lines of the table.

pairs.left: between two machines in the same zone

prompt: A student types `aws ec2 describe-regions` in a new terminal and gets `aws: command not found`. Which single line fixes it?
hint: It is typed in every terminal.

choices.text: `moto_server -p 4567`
choices.why: That starts moto, in the other terminal, and would not be found either: it lives in the virtual environment.

choices.text: `source ~/aws/env.sh`
choices.why: Right. It puts `~/.local/bin` on the path and switches on the virtual environment, among the rest.

choices.text: `./aws/install -i ~/.local/aws-cli -b ~/.local/bin`
choices.why: The command line is installed; installing it again changes nothing about this terminal's path.

choices.text: `export AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=http://localhost:4567`
choices.why: That tells `aws` where to send requests, once it is found. The shell has not found it yet.
